claims.quote: Servicers must comply with applicable law in connection with [their] management of escrow accounts, including collecting, holding, and escrowing funds on behalf of each borrower in accordance with RESPA (12 [U.S.C.] 2609) and Regulation X (12 CFR 1024.17 and 10024.34).
claims.summary: Servicers must comply with applicable law regarding escrow account management, including collecting, holding, and escrowing funds in accordance with RESPA and Regulation X.

claims.quote: Servicers must closely monitor property taxing authorities and individual insurance contracts to ensure that escrow calculations are accurate and that insurance policies have not lapsed.
claims.summary: Servicers must closely monitor property taxing authorities and insurance contracts to ensure accurate escrow calculations and that insurance policies have not lapsed.

claims.quote: Servicers also should ensure compliance with legal requirements regarding the cessation of escrow withholding for [private market insurance] on serviced loans.
claims.summary: Servicers should ensure compliance with legal requirements regarding the cessation of escrow withholding for private market insurance on serviced loans.

claims.quote: 12 U.S.C. 1828(o) instructs the Federal banking agencies to ``adopt uniform regulations prescribing standards for extensions of credit'' related to certain real estate transactions.
claims.summary: Federal banking agencies must adopt uniform regulations prescribing standards for extensions of credit related to certain real estate transactions.

claims.quote: 12 U.S.C. 371(a) clearly states that national banks' real estate lending powers are subject both to 12 U.S.C. 1828(o) ``and such restrictions and requirements as the Comptroller of the Currency may prescribe by regulation or order'' (emphasis added).
claims.summary: National banks' real estate lending powers are subject to both 12 U.S.C. 1828(o) and regulations prescribed by the Comptroller of the Currency.

claims.quote: A reading of the statute that section 1828(o) is the controlling basis for adopting regulations would render the Comptroller's concurrent rulemaking authority as surplusage--``[i]t is a cardinal principle of statutory construction that a statute ought, upon the whole, to be so construed that, if it can be prevented, no clause, sentence, or word shall be superfluous, void, or insignificant.''
claims.summary: The Comptroller of the Currency's concurrent rulemaking authority must not be rendered surplusage by interpreting section 1828(o) as the sole basis for adopting regulations.

claims.quote: HOLA provides Federal savings associations broad powers to invest in, sell, or otherwise deal in residential real property loans, subject to regulations issued by the Comptroller.
claims.summary: Federal savings associations have broad powers to invest in, sell, or otherwise deal in residential real property loans, subject to regulations issued by the Comptroller.

claims.quote: HOLA also provides the OCC with broad authority to prescribe rules and regulations to provide for the organization, incorporation, examination, operation, and regulation of Federal savings associations and to specify their powers to invest in, sell, or otherwise deal in various loans and other investments.
claims.summary: The OCC has broad authority to prescribe rules and regulations for the organization, incorporation, examination, operation, and regulation of Federal savings associations, as well as to specify their powers to invest in, sell, or otherwise deal in various loans and other investments.

claims.quote: HOLA also authorizes Federal savings associations to engage in nonresidential real estate lending not in excess of 400 percent of capital or certain greater amounts as determined by the Comptroller, subject to regulations issued by the Comptroller.
claims.summary: Federal savings associations are authorized to engage in nonresidential real estate lending up to 400 percent of capital or certain greater amounts as determined by the Comptroller, subject to regulations issued by the Comptroller.

claims.quote: 12 U.S.C. 1464(a); see also Fid. Fed. Sav. & Loan Ass'n v. de la Cuesta, 458 U.S. 141, 145 (1982) (``Pursuant to this authorization [12 U.S.C. 1464(a)], the [Federal Home Loan Bank] Board has promulgated regulations governing the powers and operations of every Federal savings and loan association from its cradle to its corporate grave.'' (citation modified)). This authority to promulgate regulations for Federal savings associations was ultimately transferred to the OCC. 12 U.S.C. 5412(b)(2)(B).
claims.summary: The OCC has the authority to promulgate regulations governing the powers and operations of Federal savings associations, as transferred from the Federal Home Loan Bank Board under 12 U.S.C. 5412(b)(2)(B).

claims.quote: Since the earliest days of the Federal banking system, courts have held that banks have wide latitude in managing and protecting property acquired in the usual course of banking, even where such activities are not otherwise permissible.
claims.summary: Courts have held that banks have wide latitude in managing and protecting property acquired in the usual course of banking, even where such activities are not otherwise permissible.

claims.quote: Courts have also explicitly linked the power to lend as inextricably bound up in the power to foreclose on collateral.
claims.summary: Courts have explicitly linked the power to lend as inextricably bound up in the power to foreclose on collateral.

claims.quote: It requires disclosures as to the nature and purposes of escrow accounts,
claims.summary: Lenders must provide disclosures regarding the nature and purposes of escrow accounts.

claims.quote: mandates the provision of free annual escrow account statements,
claims.summary: Lenders must provide free annual escrow account statements.

claims.quote: requires amounts in escrow accounts be paid timely as they become due and any funds remaining in such accounts after the loan is repaid be promptly returned to the borrower,
claims.summary: Lenders must pay amounts in escrow accounts timely as they become due and return any remaining funds to the borrower after the loan is repaid.

claims.quote: establishes proportional caps on the total amounts that may be collected from borrowers in escrow accounts.
claims.summary: Lenders must establish proportional caps on the total amounts that may be collected from borrowers in escrow accounts.

claims.quote: national banks are permitted to engage in the business of banking more generally and ``all such incidental powers as shall be necessary to carry on the business of banking.''
claims.summary: National banks are permitted to engage in the business of banking more generally and all such incidental powers as shall be necessary to carry on the business of banking.

claims.quote: The exercise of the Comptroller's discretion, however, must be kept within reasonable bounds.
claims.summary: The exercise of the Comptroller's discretion must be kept within reasonable bounds.

claims.quote: The OCC considers the following factors when determining whether an activity that is not explicitly enumerated in 12 U.S.C. 24(Seventh) is nonetheless part of the business of banking:
claims.summary: The OCC considers specific factors when determining whether an activity not explicitly enumerated in 12 U.S.C. 24(Seventh) is part of the business of banking.

claims.quote: (i) Whether the activity is the functional equivalent to, or a logical outgrowth of, a recognized banking activity;
claims.summary: The OCC must consider whether the activity is the functional equivalent to, or a logical outgrowth of, a recognized banking activity.

claims.quote: (ii) Whether the activity strengthens the bank by benefiting its customers or its business;
claims.summary: The OCC must consider whether the activity strengthens the bank by benefiting its customers or its business.

claims.quote: (iii) Whether the activity involves risks similar in nature to those already assumed by banks; and
claims.summary: The OCC must consider whether the activity involves risks similar in nature to those already assumed by banks.

claims.quote: (iv) Whether the activity is authorized for State-chartered banks.
claims.summary: The OCC must consider whether the activity is authorized for State-chartered banks.

claims.quote: The weight accorded to each factor depends on the facts and circumstances of each case.
claims.summary: The weight given to each factor in determining whether an activity is incidental to the business of banking depends on the specific facts and circumstances of each case.

claims.quote: An activity is ``incidental to the business of banking if it is convenient or useful to an activity that is specifically authorized for national banks or to an activity that is otherwise part of the business of banking.''
claims.summary: An activity is considered incidental to the business of banking if it is convenient or useful to an authorized activity or part of the business of banking.

claims.quote: The OCC considers the following factors in such analysis: ``(i) Whether the activity facilitates the production or delivery of a bank's products or services, enhances the bank's ability to sell or market its products or services, or improves the effectiveness or efficiency of the bank's operations, in light of risks presented, innovations, strategies, techniques and new technologies for producing and delivering financial products and services; and (ii) Whether the activity enables the bank to use capacity acquired for its banking operations or otherwise avoid economic loss or waste.''
claims.summary: The OCC considers factors such as whether an activity facilitates the production or delivery of a bank's products or services, enhances its ability to sell or market them, or improves the effectiveness or efficiency of operations, and whether it enables the bank to use capacity acquired for banking operations or avoid economic loss or waste.

claims.quote: Flexibility to exercise a national bank's business judgment as to how to structure its escrow operations and whether and to what extent to offer any compensation to customers is a clear logical outgrowth of national banks' other powers to manage and protect collateral.
claims.summary: National banks have flexibility in structuring their escrow operations and determining the extent of compensation to offer customers, as it is a logical outgrowth of their powers to manage and protect collateral.

claims.quote: It is a fundamental precept of banking that the bank has flexibility in determining what, if any, interest is paid on the funds held in customer accounts, including escrow accounts.
claims.summary: Banks have the flexibility to determine what, if any, interest is paid on funds held in customer accounts, including escrow accounts.

claims.quote: Finally, roughly three quarters of States permit State-chartered banks flexibility to exercise their business judgment as to how to structure the financing of their escrow operations for residential real estate lending, either explicitly SSS or implicitly through silence on the subject,TTT and the OCC is not aware of any State restricting this flexibility with regards to commercial real estate lending.
claims.summary: State-chartered banks have flexibility to structure escrow operations for residential real estate lending, either explicitly or implicitly through silence.

claims.quote: See Iowa Code sec. 524.905(2) (2025) (``A bank receiving funds in escrow pursuant to an escrow agreement executed in connection with a loan . . . may pay interest to the borrower on those funds.'' (emphasis added)).
claims.summary: A bank receiving funds in escrow pursuant to an escrow agreement executed in connection with a loan may pay interest to the borrower on those funds.

claims.quote: The States and territories that require their own State-chartered banks to pay specified interest amounts on mortgage-escrow accounts include California (Cal. Civ. Code sec. 2954.8 (2025)), Connecticut (Conn. Gen. Stat. sec. 49-2a (2025)), Guam (11 Guam Code Ann. sec. 106103 (2024)); Maine (Me. Rev. Stat. Ann. tit. 9-B, sec. 429; id. tit. 33, sec. 504), Maryland (Md. Code Ann., Com. Law secs. 12-109, 12-109.2 (2025)), Massachusetts (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 183, sec. 61 (2025)), Minnesota (Minn. Stat. Ann. sec. 47.20, subd. 9 (2025)), New Hampshire (N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. sec. 383-B:3-303(a)(7)(E) (2025)), New York (N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law sec. 5-601 (2025)), Oregon (Or. Rev. Stat. secs. 86.245, 86.250 (2025)), Rhode Island (19 R.I. Gen. Laws sec. 19-9-2 (2025)), U.S. Virgin Islands (V.I. Code tit. 9, sec. 67 2025), Utah (Utah Code Ann. sec. 7-17-3 (2025)), Vermont (Vt. Stat. Ann. tit. 8, sec. 10404 (2025)), and Wisconsin (Wis. Stat. secs. 138.051, 138.052 (2025)).
claims.summary: The States and territories that require their own State-chartered banks to pay specified interest amounts on mortgage-escrow accounts include California, Connecticut, Guam, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, U.S. Virgin Islands, Utah, Vermont, and Wisconsin.

claims.quote: Several commenters rejected this line of reasoning on the basis that 12 U.S.C. 93a merely allows the OCC to carry out its responsibilities and does not carry with it authority to confer on national banks powers that they do not have under existing law. Even assuming this assertion is accurate, the OCC's rule is fully consistent with it.
claims.summary: The OCC's rule is fully consistent with 12 U.S.C. 93a, which allows the OCC to carry out its responsibilities without conferring powers that national banks do not have under existing law.

claims.quote: The preamble extensively discusses the existing and historical power of national banks to exercise flexibility to make business judgments in structuring escrow accounts under 12 U.S.C. 24(Seventh). The final rule merely clarifies longstanding and recognized real estate lending powers that banks have exercised under existing law.
claims.summary: The final rule clarifies longstanding and recognized real estate lending powers that national banks have exercised under existing law.

claims.quote: Other commenters stated that the agency's rulemaking authority is limited based on 12 U.S.C. 25b, a statute that does not concern national banks' real estate lending powers. Specifically, these commenters pointed to the OCC's concurrent proposed preemption determination related to State interest-on-escrow laws UUU and asserted that the proposed rule on bank powers was merely pretext for achieving other aims.
claims.summary: Commenters asserted that the proposed rule on bank powers was merely pretext for achieving other aims, based on the OCC's concurrent proposed preemption determination related to State interest-on-escrow laws.

claims.quote: As explained above, this final rule is clearly supported by the plain meaning and judicial history of the statutory authorities cited. Assertions that these authorities are somehow limited by either context or unrelated statutes that do not specifically limit application of the cited authorities are not statutorily grounded. This final rule is a permissible exercise of the OCC's congressionally granted authority to clarify national banks' longstanding and recognized real estate lending powers.
claims.summary: The final rule is a permissible exercise of the OCC's congressionally granted authority to clarify national banks' longstanding and recognized real estate lending powers.
The OCC's concurrent proposed preemption determination related to State interest-on-escrow laws is referenced as 90 FR 61093 (Dec. 30, 2025).

claims.quote: Relevant case law requires that agencies disclose technical studies, when such studies form the basis of a proposed rule, to give the public adequate opportunity to provide comment.
claims.summary: Agencies must disclose technical studies when they form the basis of a proposed rule to allow the public to provide comment.

claims.quote: the final rule amends the OCC's real estate lending and appraisals regulations applicable to national banks and its lending and investment regulations applicable to Federal savings associations to add a definition of ``escrow account,'' expressly codify banks' power to establish and maintain escrow accounts, and to clarify that the terms and conditions of escrow accounts, including the extent of any compensation paid to customers, are business decisions to be made by each bank.
claims.summary: The final rule adds a definition of 'escrow account,' codifies banks' power to establish and maintain escrow accounts, and clarifies that the terms and conditions of escrow accounts, including compensation paid to customers, are business decisions to be made by each bank.

claims.quote: the final rule defines an ``escrow account'' used by national banks as an account established in connection with a loan or extension of credit secured by a lien on interest in real estate in which the borrower places funds for the purpose of assuring payment of taxes, insurance premiums, or other charges with respect to the property.
claims.summary: The final rule defines an 'escrow account' used by national banks as an account established in connection with a loan or extension of credit secured by a lien on interest in real estate in which the borrower places funds for the purpose of assuring payment of taxes, insurance premiums, or other charges with respect to the property.

claims.quote: the final rule defines ``escrow accounts'' in substantially similar terms in the context of Federal savings associations.
claims.summary: The final rule defines 'escrow accounts' in substantially similar terms in the context of Federal savings associations.

claims.quote: the final rule codifies national banks' escrow powers, including the flexibility such banks have as to how to organize and manage escrow accounts.
claims.summary: The final rule codifies national banks' escrow powers, including the flexibility such banks have as to how to organize and manage escrow accounts.

claims.quote: the final rule codifies that (1) the powers of national banks include establishing and maintaining escrow accounts in connection with real estate loans; and (2) the terms and conditions of such escrow accounts (including, but not limited to, the investment of escrowed funds, fees assessed for the provision of such accounts, and whether and to what extent interest or other compensation is calculated and paid to customers whose funds are placed in the escrow account) are business decisions to be made by each national bank in its discretion.
claims.summary: The final rule codifies that (1) the powers of national banks include establishing and maintaining escrow accounts in connection with real estate loans; and (2) the terms and conditions of such escrow accounts (including, but not limited to, the investment of escrowed funds, fees assessed for the provision of such accounts, and whether and to what extent interest or other compensation is calculated and paid to customers whose funds are placed in the escrow account) are business decisions to be made by each national bank in its discretion.

claims.quote: the final rule codifies these powers in the context of Federal savings associations in substantially similar terms.
claims.summary: The final rule codifies these powers in the context of Federal savings associations in substantially similar terms.

claims.quote: prohibiting unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce
claims.summary: Prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.

claims.quote: requiring national banks to adopt and maintain written policies that establish appropriate limits and standards for real estate lending, including that they be consistent with safe and sound banking practices
claims.summary: Requires national banks to adopt and maintain written policies for real estate lending that are consistent with safe and sound banking practices.

claims.quote: requiring banks to establish loan administration procedures that address escrow account administration
claims.summary: Requires banks to establish loan administration procedures that address escrow account administration.

claims.quote: no agency may conduct or sponsor, nor is the respondent required to respond to, an information collection unless it displays a currently valid Office of Management and Budget (OMB) control number
claims.summary: Prohibits an agency from conducting or sponsoring an information collection unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.

claims.quote: no PRA submissions to OMB will be made with respect to this final rule
claims.summary: Prohibits the OCC from making PRA submissions to OMB with respect to this final rule.

claims.quote: the agency, in connection with a final rule, to prepare a final regulatory flexibility analysis describing the impact of the rule on small entities
claims.summary: Requires an agency to prepare a final regulatory flexibility analysis describing the impact of the rule on small entities.

claims.quote: this analysis is not required if an agency certifies that the rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities and publishes its certification and a short explanatory statement in the Federal Register along with its rule
claims.summary: Requires an agency to certify that the rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities and to publish its certification and a short explanatory statement in the Federal Register.

claims.quote: the OCC classifies the economic impact on an individual small entity as significant if the total estimated impact in one year is greater than 5 percent of the small entity's total annual salaries and benefits or greater than 2.5 percent of the small entity's total non-interest expense.
claims.summary: The OCC classifies the economic impact on an individual small entity as significant based on specific thresholds.

claims.quote: the OCC considers 5 percent or more of OCC-supervised small entities to be a substantial number, and at present, 30 OCC-supervised small entities would constitute a substantial number.
claims.summary: The OCC considers 5 percent or more of OCC-supervised small entities to be a substantial number, with 30 entities currently being considered substantial.

claims.quote: the OCC certifies that the final rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities supervised by the OCC.
claims.summary: The OCC certifies that the final rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.

claims.affected_party: State, local, and tribal governments; private sector
claims.quote: the OCC has analyzed the final rule under the factors in the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA).
claims.summary: The OCC has analyzed the final rule under the factors in the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995.

claims.affected_party: State, local, and tribal governments; private sector
claims.quote: the OCC considers whether the final rule includes a Federal mandate that may result in the expenditure by State, local, and tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $193 million or more in any one year.
claims.summary: The OCC considers whether the final rule includes a Federal mandate that may result in the expenditure of $193 million or more annually by State, local, and tribal governments or the private sector.

claims.affected_party: State, local, and tribal governments; private sector
claims.quote: the OCC has not prepared the written statement described in section 202 of the UMRA.
claims.summary: The OCC has not prepared the written statement described in section 202 of the UMRA.

claims.affected_party: depository institutions; customers of depository institutions
claims.quote: the OCC must consider, consistent with principles of safety and soundness and the public interest, (1) any administrative burdens that the final rule would place on depository institutions, including small depository institutions and customers of depository institutions and (2) the benefits of the final rule.
claims.summary: The OCC must consider administrative burdens and benefits of the final rule on depository institutions and their customers.

claims.quote: This rulemaking will not impose any reporting, disclosure, or other requirements on insured depository institutions.
claims.summary: This rulemaking will not impose any reporting, disclosure, or other requirements on insured depository institutions.

claims.affected_party: Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), OMB
claims.quote: Executive Order 12866, titled ``Regulatory Planning and Review,'' as amended, requires the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), OMB, to determine whether a final rule is a ``significant regulatory action'' prior to the disclosure of the final rule to the public.
claims.summary: OIRA must determine if a final rule is a significant regulatory action before disclosing it to the public.

claims.quote: If OIRA finds the final rule to be a ``significant regulatory action,'' Executive Order 12866 requires the OCC to conduct a cost-benefit analysis of the final rule and for OIRA to conduct a review of the final rule prior to publication in the Federal Register.
claims.summary: If the final rule is a significant regulatory action, the OCC must conduct a cost-benefit analysis, and OIRA must conduct a review before publication in the Federal Register.

claims.quote: Executive Order 14192, titled ``Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation,'' requires that an agency, unless prohibited by law, identify at least 10 existing regulations to be repealed when the agency publicly proposes for notice and comment or otherwise promulgates a new regulation with total costs greater than zero.
claims.summary: An agency must identify at least 10 existing regulations to be repealed when proposing or promulgating a new regulation with total costs greater than zero.

claims.quote: Executive Order 14192 further requires that new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.
claims.summary: New incremental costs from new regulations must be offset by eliminating existing costs from at least 10 prior regulations, to the extent permitted by law.

claims.quote: For purposes of the Congressional Review Act, OMB makes a determination as to whether a final rule constitutes a ``major'' rule.
claims.summary: OMB must determine whether a final rule constitutes a ``major'' rule under the Congressional Review Act.

claims.quote: If a rule is deemed a ``major rule'' by the OMB, the Congressional Review Act generally provides that the rule may not take effect until at least 60 days following its publication.
claims.summary: If a rule is deemed a ``major rule'' by OMB, it may not take effect until at least 60 days after its publication.

claims.quote: the OCC will submit the final rule and other appropriate reports to Congress and the Government Accountability Office for review.
claims.summary: The OCC must submit the final rule and other appropriate reports to Congress and the Government Accountability Office for review.

claims.quote: The OCC received approximately 20 comments on its proposed preemption determination from a variety of stakeholders, including banks, trade associations, members of Congress, consumer groups, academics, State representatives, and individuals.

claims.quote: The OCC agrees that these interest-on-escrow laws both have substantively equivalent terms to New York's interest-on-escrow law, and the OCC has incorporated these laws into its preemption determination.

claims.quote: The OCC is issuing this final preemption determination, which concludes that (1) the National Bank Act preempts section 5-601 of New York's General Obligations Law, the State's interest-on-escrow law; (2) thirteen other States have laws with substantively equivalent terms; and (3) these substantively equivalent State laws are also preempted.
claims.summary: The OCC is issuing a final preemption determination that concludes the National Bank Act preempts section 5-601 of New York's General Obligations Law, thirteen other States have laws with substantively equivalent terms, and these laws are also preempted.

claims.quote: Section 5-601 of New York's General Obligations Law requires ``mortgage investing institutions'' to pay ``dividends or interest at a rate of not less than two per centum per year . . . or a rate prescribed by the [New York] superintendent of financial services'' on escrow account balances.
claims.summary: New York's General Obligations Law requires mortgage investing institutions to pay a minimum interest rate on escrow account balances.

claims.quote: This statutory obligation applies whenever the institution ``maintains an escrow account pursuant to any agreement executed in connection with a mortgage on any one to six family residence occupied by the owner or on any property owned by a cooperative apartment corporation'' located in New York.
claims.summary: The statutory obligation applies when the institution maintains an escrow account for a mortgage on a one to six family residence or property owned by a cooperative apartment corporation in New York.

claims.quote: This New York law also requires the institution to credit the interest to the escrow account on a quarterly basis, and it generally prohibits the assessment of a service charge in connection with maintaining an escrow account.
claims.summary: The New York law requires institutions to credit interest to the escrow account quarterly and generally prohibits assessing service charges for maintaining an escrow account.

claims.quote: This assessment may include consideration of Barnett and its antecedents and be based on ``the text and structure of the laws, comparison to other precedents, and common sense.''
claims.summary: Courts must consider the text and structure of the laws, comparison to other precedents, and common sense when applying the Barnett standard.

claims.quote: courts addressing preemption questions in this context must do as Barnett Bank did and likewise take account of those prior decisions of this Court and similar precedents.
claims.summary: Courts must take account of prior decisions of this Court and similar precedents when addressing preemption questions.

claims.quote: Finding that the State law limitations would interfere with this flexibility, which was critical to the Federal scheme, the Fidelity Court concluded that the State law was preempted.
claims.summary: Courts must determine if state laws interfere with federal flexibility critical to the federal scheme and conclude whether the state law is preempted.

claims.quote: Because the State law interfered with national banks' ability to exercise these powers ``effectively'' and ``efficiently,'' it was preempted.
claims.summary: Courts must determine if state laws interfere with national banks' ability to exercise federal powers effectively and efficiently, and conclude whether the state law is preempted.

claims.quote: the Supreme Court has also recognized that when a State law does not prevent or significantly interfere with the national bank's exercise of its powers, it is not preempted.
claims.summary: A state law that does not prevent or significantly interfere with the national bank's exercise of its powers is not preempted.

claims.quote: the Supreme Court found that the Kentucky law was not preempted, including because it applied a rule that was as ``old as the common law itself.''
claims.summary: A state law that applies a rule as old as the common law is not preempted.

claims.quote: the State law addressed the transfer and devolution of property in the State, a kind of generally applicable State ``infrastructure'' law that is typically not preempted.
claims.summary: A state law addressing the transfer and devolution of property in the state, as a generally applicable infrastructure law, is typically not preempted.

claims.quote: national banks are subject to general State laws in their ``dealings and contracts,'' unless those laws expressly conflict with Federal law, frustrate the purpose of national banks, or impair their ability to efficiently exercise their Federally authorized powers.
claims.summary: National banks are subject to general state laws in their dealings and contracts unless those laws expressly conflict with federal law, frustrate the purpose of national banks, or impair their ability to efficiently exercise their federally authorized powers.

claims.quote: the McClellan Court held that the State law was not preempted.
claims.summary: A state law that is generally applicable and does not impose greater conditions or restrictions on national banks than on other citizens is not preempted.

claims.quote: the Supreme Court held that a Kentucky tax law was not preempted.
claims.summary: A state tax law that does not preempt national banks is not preempted.

claims.quote: the Court also stated that the State law ``in no manner hinder[ed]'' the national bank and imposed ``no greater interference with the functions of the bank than any other legal proceeding.''
claims.summary: A state law that does not hinder the national bank and imposes no greater interference with its functions than any other legal proceeding is not preempted.

claims.quote: a State law prevents or significantly interferes with a Federal power when it interferes with critical flexibility granted to a national bank under Federal law, interferes with a national bank's effectiveness or efficiency in exercising its Federal power, or qualifies a Federal power in an unusual way.
claims.summary: State laws that prevent or significantly interfere with a Federal power by interfering with critical flexibility granted to a national bank under Federal law, interfering with a national bank's effectiveness or efficiency in exercising its Federal power, or qualifying a Federal power in an unusual way are prohibited.

claims.quote: generally applicable infrastructure laws typically apply to national banks, unless they prevent or significantly interfere with a national, bank's exercise of its Federally authorized powers.
claims.summary: Generally applicable infrastructure laws typically apply to national banks, unless they prevent or significantly interfere with a national bank's exercise of its Federally authorized powers.

claims.quote: A ``preemption determination'' refers to an OCC regulation or order that concludes that a State consumer financial law is preempted in accordance with the Barnett standard under section 25b(b)(1)(B).
claims.summary: The OCC must conclude that a State consumer financial law is preempted in accordance with the Barnett standard under section 25b(b)(1)(B).

claims.quote: section 25b codified the Barnett standard, expressly recognized the OCC's role in preemption, and established procedural requirements for OCC ``preemption determinations.''
claims.summary: The OCC must follow procedural requirements for preemption determinations under section 25b.

claims.quote: A State consumer financial law is ``a State law that does not directly or indirectly discriminate against national banks and that directly and specifically regulates the manner, content, or terms and conditions of any financial transaction (as may be authorized for national banks to engage in), or any account related thereto, with respect to a consumer.''
claims.summary: A State consumer financial law must not directly or indirectly discriminate against national banks and must directly and specifically regulate the manner, content, or terms and conditions of any financial transaction authorized for national banks to engage in, or any account related thereto, with respect to a consumer.

claims.quote: the OCC must first consult with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) and take its views into account.

claims.quote: the terms and conditions of any such escrow account, including the investment of escrowed funds, fees assessed for the provision of such accounts, or whether and to what extent interest or other compensation is calculated and paid to customers whose funds are placed in the escrow account, are business decisions to be made by each national bank in its discretion.

claims.quote: These rules implement provisions to protect consumers from surprise medical bills for emergency services, non-emergency services furnished by nonparticipating providers for patient visits to participating facilities in certain circumstances, and air ambulance services furnished by nonparticipating providers of air ambulance services.
claims.summary: Rules are implemented to protect consumers from surprise medical bills for emergency services, non-emergency services furnished by nonparticipating providers for patient visits to participating facilities in certain circumstances, and air ambulance services furnished by nonparticipating providers of air ambulance services.

claims.affected_party: plans and issuers, providers, facilities, and providers of air ambulance services
claims.quote: These rules also implement provisions to establish a Federal IDR process to determine payment amounts when there is a dispute between plans or issuers and providers, facilities, or providers of air ambulance services about the out-of-network rate for these services in cases where a specified State law or an applicable All-Payer Model Agreement does not provide a method for determining the total amount payable.
claims.summary: Rules implement provisions to establish a Federal IDR process to determine payment amounts when there is a dispute between plans or issuers and providers, facilities, or providers of air ambulance services about the out-of-network rate for these services in cases where a specified State law or an applicable All-Payer Model Agreement does not provide a method for determining the total amount payable.

claims.affected_party: plans and issuers (including grandfathered health plans), health care providers, facilities, and providers of air ambulance services
claims.quote: The July 2021 interim final rules and October 2021 interim final rules generally apply to plans and issuers (including grandfathered health plans) for plan years (in the individual market, policy years) beginning on or after January 1, 2022, and to health care providers, facilities, and providers of air ambulance services for items and services furnished during plan years (in the individual market, policy years) beginning on or after January 1, 2022.
claims.summary: The July 2021 and October 2021 interim final rules apply to plans and issuers for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2022, and to health care providers, facilities, and air ambulance providers for items and services furnished during those plan years.

claims.quote: The August 2022 final rules became effective October 25, 2022, and are applicable for items and services provided or furnished on or after October 25, 2022, for plan years (in the individual market, policy years) beginning on or after January 1, 2022.
claims.summary: The August 2022 final rules became effective on October 25, 2022, and apply to items and services provided or furnished on or after that date for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2022.

claims.quote: The disclosure requirements at 45 CFR 149.430 regarding patient protections against balance billing are applicable as of January 1, 2022.
claims.summary: The disclosure requirements at 45 CFR 149.430 regarding patient protections against balance billing are applicable as of January 1, 2022.

claims.quote: A dispute is not eligible for the Federal IDR process unless it concerns an item or service that meets the definition of a qualified IDR item or service. 29 CFR 2590.716-8(a)(2)(xi) and 45 CFR 149.510 (a)(2)(xi).
claims.summary: A dispute is not eligible for the Federal IDR process unless it concerns an item or service that meets the definition of a qualified IDR item or service.

claims.quote: Disputes are also ineligible when the disputing parties initiate the Federal IDR process after failing to satisfy the 30-business-day open negotiation period requirements specified under 29 CFR 2590.716-8(b)(1) and 45 CFR 149.510(b)(1) or after 4 business days after the end of the 30-business-day open negotiation period as specified under 29 CFR 2590.716-8(b)(2)(i) and 45 CFR 149.510(b)(2)(i).
claims.summary: Disputes are ineligible if the disputing parties initiate the Federal IDR process after failing to satisfy the 30-business-day open negotiation period requirements or after 4 business days after the end of the 30-business-day open negotiation period.

claims.quote: 29 CFR 2590.716-8(c)(3)(i)(B) and 45 CFR 149.510(c)(3)(i)(B). The District Court vacated the batching provisions of 45 CFR 149.510(c)(3)(i)(C), 26 CFR 54.9816-8T(c)(3)(i)(C), and 29 CFR 2590.716-8(c)(3)(i)(C) in Tex. Med. Ass'n v. U.S. Dep't of Health & Hum. Servs., Case No. 6:23-cv-59-JDK (E.D. Tex. Aug. 3, 2023) (TMA IV).
claims.summary: The batching provisions of 45 CFR 149.510(c)(3)(i)(C), 26 CFR 54.9816-8T(c)(3)(i)(C), and 29 CFR 2590.716-8(c)(3)(i)(C) were vacated by the District Court.

Disputes are ineligible if the disputing parties incorrectly bundle items or services, such as submitting an emergency room facility code with various item and service codes included as line items instead of properly submitting a single service code.

claims.quote: The Departments have implemented Federal IDR portal system enhancements, such as enabling non-initiating parties to submit supporting documentation to contest dispute eligibility within their response to the notice of IDR initiation and requiring non-initiating parties to attest to the health plan type.
claims.summary: Non-initiating parties must submit supporting documentation to contest dispute eligibility within their response to the notice of IDR initiation and must attest to the health plan type.

claims.quote: requiring that these parties share specific information before initiating the Federal IDR process, including by providing No Surprises Act-specific claim adjustment reason codes (CARCs) and remittance advice remark codes (RARCs) with a remittance advice.
claims.summary: Plans, issuers, and providers must share specific information before initiating the Federal IDR process, including providing No Surprises Act-specific claim adjustment reason codes (CARCs) and remittance advice remark codes (RARCs) with a remittance advice.

claims.quote: amend the information that must be disclosed about the QPA.
claims.summary: Plans, issuers, and providers must disclose amended information about the QPA.

claims.quote: require plans and issuers to register with the Federal IDR portal to facilitate identification of the parties to a dispute and determine whether coverage of an item or service that is the subject of the dispute is subject to a specified State law, an All-Payer Model Agreement, or the Federal IDR process for determining the out-of-network rate.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers must register with the Federal IDR portal to facilitate identification of the parties to a dispute and determine whether coverage of an item or service that is the subject of the dispute is subject to a specified State law, an All-Payer Model Agreement, or the Federal IDR process for determining the out-of-network rate.

claims.quote: amend to the content requirements of the standard open negotiation notice, establish requirements related to an open negotiation response notice, and clarify the timing for when the open negotiation period begins.
claims.summary: Plans, issuers, and providers must amend the content requirements of the standard open negotiation notice, establish requirements related to an open negotiation response notice, and clarify the timing for when the open negotiation period begins.

claims.quote: include amendments to the notice of IDR initiation and new requirements for the initiation response from the non-initiating party.
claims.summary: The non-initiating party must comply with amendments to the notice of IDR initiation and new requirements for the initiation response.

claims.quote: proposed establishing a new process for providing and receiving notices related to the IDR process.
claims.summary: A new process for providing and receiving notices related to the IDR process was proposed.

claims.quote: The 2023 proposed rules also proposed to establish a standard process for disputes to be withdrawn from the Federal IDR process.
claims.summary: Establish a standard process for disputes to be withdrawn from the Federal IDR process.

claims.quote: The Departments also proposed amendments to adjust the timeframe for submission of offers and payment determination.
claims.summary: Adjust the timeframe for submission of offers and payment determination.

claims.quote: The proposed rule included amendments related to the collection of certified IDR entity fees and administrative fees.
claims.summary: Amendments related to the collection of certified IDR entity fees and administrative fees.

claims.quote: The Departments proposed a reduced administrative fee amount for low-dollar disputes to address access concerns by certain interested parties that regularly provide services with low-dollar values.
claims.summary: Propose a reduced administrative fee amount for low-dollar disputes.

claims.quote: The Departments also proposed reduced administrative fee amounts for non-initiating parties in cases of ineligible disputes as well as pursuing Federal debt collection of the administrative fee from parties that do not pay as required.
claims.summary: Propose reduced administrative fee amounts for non-initiating parties in cases of ineligible disputes and pursue Federal debt collection of the administrative fee from parties that do not pay as required.

claims.quote: The Departments proposed to amend requirements related to batched items and services and bundled payment arrangements.
claims.summary: Amend requirements related to batched items and services and bundled payment arrangements.

claims.quote: The proposed rules also proposed to expand upon situations in which timeframes may be waived due to extenuating circumstances.
claims.summary: Expand upon situations in which timeframes may be waived due to extenuating circumstances.

claims.quote: The Departments shall provide that, in the case of items and services which are included by a provider or facility as part of a bundled payment, such items and services may be part of a single determination.
claims.summary: The Departments must provide that items and services included in a bundled payment may be part of a single determination.

claims.affected_party: providers, facilities, providers of air ambulance services, plans, and issuers
claims.quote: The October 2021 interim final rules specify that in the case of qualified IDR items and services billed by a provider, facility, or provider of air ambulance services as part of a bundled payment arrangement, or if a plan or issuer makes or denies an initial payment as a bundled payment, the qualified IDR items and services may be submitted as part of one dispute and are subject to the rules for batched disputes and the certified IDR entity fee for single disputes.
claims.summary: Qualified IDR items and services billed as part of a bundled payment arrangement may be submitted as part of one dispute and are subject to batched dispute rules and certified IDR entity fees for single disputes.

claims.quote: The Departments provided a definition for a bundled arrangement in the August 2022 Technical Assistance for Certified IDR Entities.
claims.summary: The Departments must provide a definition for a bundled arrangement in the August 2022 Technical Assistance for Certified IDR Entities.

claims.quote: The 2023 proposed rules proposed to codify the definition set forth in the August 2022 Technical Assistance for Certified IDR Entities.
claims.summary: The 2023 proposed rules proposed to codify the definition provided in the August 2022 Technical Assistance for Certified IDR Entities.

claims.affected_party: provider, facility, or provider of air ambulance services; plan or issuer
claims.quote: a provider, facility, or provider of air ambulance services bills for multiple items or services furnished to a single patient under a single service code that represents multiple items or services (for example, a diagnostic related group (DRG) code); or (2) a plan or issuer makes an initial payment or notice of denial of payment to a provider, facility, or provider of air ambulance services under a single service code that represents multiple items or services furnished to a single patient (for example, a DRG code).
claims.summary: Providers or facilities must bill for multiple items or services under a single service code, and plans or issuers must make initial payments or denials under such codes.

claims.quote: the Departments proposed to remove the language under 26 CFR 54.9816-8T(c)(3)(ii), 29 CFR 2590.716-8(c)(3)(ii), and 45 CFR 149.510(c)(3)(ii) stating that a bundled payment arrangement is subject to the rules for batched disputes.
claims.summary: The Departments proposed to remove the language stating that bundled payment arrangements are subject to the rules for batched disputes.

claims.quote: the Departments are finalizing the definition of the term ``bundled payment arrangement'' at 26 CFR 54.9816-3, 29 CFR 2590.716-3, and 45 CFR 149.30 as proposed.
claims.summary: The Departments are finalizing the definition of ``bundled payment arrangement'' as proposed.

claims.quote: the Departments did not receive any comments on the proposed amendment to remove the language under 26 CFR 54.9816-8T(c)(3)(ii), 29 CFR 2590.716-8(c)(3)(ii), and 45 CFR 149.510(c)(3)(ii) stating that a bundled payment arrangement is subject to the rules for batched disputes, and are finalizing this amendment as proposed.
claims.summary: The Departments are finalizing the amendment to remove the language stating that bundled payment arrangements are subject to the rules for batched disputes.

claims.quote: The provider shall report (or for the purpose of the Federal IDR process, the provider shall bill) the Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) code 77066 (Diagnostic mammography . . . bilateral).
claims.summary: Providers must report or bill using the specific CPT code for bilateral mammography.

claims.quote: The provider should not submit CPT code 77065 (Diagnostic mammography . . . unilateral) with 2 UOS or CPT code 77065 LT (unilateral left breast mammography) plus CPT code 77065 RT (unilateral right breast mammography).
claims.summary: Providers must not submit separate CPT codes for unilateral mammography on both breasts.

claims.quote: Under these final rules, if the services are billed or reimbursed under one service code (CPT code 77066), all services performed under that service code (CPT codes 77065 LT and 77065 RT) may be considered a bundled payment arrangement for purposes of the Federal IDR process.
claims.summary: Providers must consider services billed under a single CPT code as a bundled payment arrangement for the Federal IDR process.

claims.quote: The definition of bundled payment arrangements under these final rules allows disputes to be bundled by a single CPT code, DRG code, or HCPCS code, provided the dispute otherwise complies with such definition.
claims.summary: Providers must bundle disputes using a single CPT, DRG, or HCPCS code if the dispute complies with the definition.

claims.quote: All ERAs must comply with the Accredited Standards Committee (ASC) X12 835 transaction standard adopted by HHS under 45 CFR 162.1602.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers must comply with the ASC X12 835 transaction standard for electronic remittance advice (ERA).

claims.quote: The HIPAA operating rule adopted at 45 CFR 162.1603(a)(4) requires plans and issuers to use a uniform set of CARCs and RARCs for defined business scenarios.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers must use a uniform set of CARCs and RARCs for defined business scenarios.

claims.quote: Any interested party can use publicly available forms to submit requests for new or modified CARCs and RARCs and accompanying explanations to the respective committees on a rolling basis.
claims.summary: Interested parties must use publicly available forms to submit requests for new or modified CARCs and RARCs and accompanying explanations to the respective committees on a rolling basis.

claims.quote: Each committee meets on a regularly scheduled, periodic basis to discuss proposed new CARCs and RARCs or modifications of existing CARCs and RARCs with the sponsors of such changes and determine whether to approve or deny the recommended change or new CARC or RARC.
claims.summary: Each committee must meet on a regularly scheduled, periodic basis to discuss proposed new CARCs and RARCs or modifications of existing CARCs and RARCs with the sponsors of such changes and determine whether to approve or deny the recommended change or new CARC or RARC.

claims.affected_party: the CARC Committee and the RARC Committee
claims.quote: Updated lists of approved CARCs and RARCs, along with an updated list of approved CARC and RARC combinations and business scenarios, are published three times each year.
claims.summary: Updated lists of approved CARCs and RARCs, along with an updated list of approved CARC and RARC combinations and business scenarios, must be published three times each year.

claims.quote: The RARC Committee has approved a set of specific RARCs that convey information related to the No Surprises Act, including which provisions apply to a claim, how cost sharing was calculated, and whether a payment for a claim was an initial or final payment.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers must use specific RARCs to convey information related to the No Surprises Act, including which provisions apply to a claim, how cost sharing was calculated, and whether a payment for a claim was an initial or final payment.

claims.quote: the No Surprises Act-specific RARCs do not address all required QPA disclosures or all data elements relevant to whether a payment dispute arising from an item or service included on a remittance advice is eligible for the Federal IDR process.
claims.summary: No Surprises Act-specific RARCs do not address all required QPA disclosures or all data elements relevant to whether a payment dispute arising from an item or service included on a remittance advice is eligible for the Federal IDR process.

claims.quote: the current standards and operating rules that govern ERA transactions under HIPAA do not include specific requirements that dictate which combinations of CARCs and RARCs must be used to communicate claim adjudication information in business scenarios anticipated by the No Surprises Act.
claims.summary: Current standards and operating rules under HIPAA do not include specific requirements dictating which combinations of CARCs and RARCs must be used to communicate claim adjudication information in business scenarios anticipated by the No Surprises Act.

claims.quote: Under section 9816(a)(2)(B)(ii) of the Code, section 716(a)(2)(B) of ERISA, and section 2799A-1(a)(2)(B)(ii) of the PHS Act, the Departments are directed to establish through rulemaking the information that a plan or issuer must share with a provider or facility when making a determination of the QPA.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers must share specific information with providers or facilities when making a determination of the QPA, as directed by sections 9816(a)(2)(B)(ii) of the Code, section 716(a)(2)(B) of ERISA, and section 2799A-1(a)(2)(B)(ii) of the PHS Act.

claims.quote: Under section 9833 of the Code, section 734 of ERISA, and section 2792 of the PHS Act, the Departments are authorized to issue such regulations as may be necessary and appropriate to carry out the provisions of chapter 100 of the Code, part 7 of ERISA, and title XXVII of the PHS Act, respectively, including the provisions directing the Departments to establish the Federal IDR process.
claims.summary: The Departments are authorized to issue regulations necessary and appropriate to carry out the provisions of chapter 100 of the Code, part 7 of ERISA, and title XXVII of the PHS Act, including establishing the Federal IDR process.

claims.quote: the July 2021 interim final rules also applied the requirement to make disclosures regarding the QPA for providers of air ambulance services.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers must make disclosures regarding the QPA for providers of air ambulance services.

claims.quote: These proposals would require plans and issuers to use CARCs and RARCs, as specified in guidance issued by the Departments, or as required under any applicable adopted standards and operating rules under 45 CFR part 162, to communicate information related to whether a claim for an item or service furnished by an entity that does not have a direct or indirect contractual relationship with the plan or issuer for the furnishing of such item or service under the plan or coverage is subject to the provisions of 26 CFR 54.9816 and 54.9817; 29 CFR 2590.716 and 2590.717; or 45 CFR part 149, subpart B, E, or F.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers must use CARCs and RARCs to communicate information related to whether a claim for an item or service is subject to specific provisions.

claims.quote: the Departments are finalizing the CARC and RARC proposal with minor modifications.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers must finalize the CARC and RARC proposal with minor modifications.

claims.quote: the requirement to use specified CARCs and RARCs under these final rules will be in addition to the disclosure requirements at 26 CFR 54.9816-6(d), 29 CFR 2590.716-6(d), and 45 CFR 149.140(d) and Federal IDR registry requirements at 26 CFR 54.9816-9, 29 CFR 2590.716-9, and 45 CFR 149.530.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers must use specified CARCs and RARCs in addition to existing disclosure and Federal IDR registry requirements.

claims.quote: The Departments proposed this approach so that CARCs and RARCs could be used to convey when the No Surprises Act does not apply to a particular item or service and reduce the submission of ineligible disputes to the Federal IDR process.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers must use CARCs and RARCs to convey when the No Surprises Act does not apply to a particular item or service to reduce ineligible disputes.

claims.quote: The Departments also proposed in the 2023 proposed rules that the requirements under 26 CFR 54.9816-6A, 29 CFR 2590.716-6A, and 45 CFR 149.100 relating to CARCs and RARCs would apply to plans and issuers when sending any paper or electronic remittance advice to entities with which they do not have a direct or indirect contractual relationship, including for items and services to which the No Surprises Act surprise billing requirements do not apply.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers must apply CARC and RARC requirements when sending remittance advice to entities without a direct or indirect contractual relationship, including for items and services not subject to the No Surprises Act.

claims.quote: These final rules do not require plans and issuers to use CARCs and RARCs on remittance advice for payments made directly to participants, beneficiaries, or enrollees--including if the remittance advice is requested by the provider that furnished the item or service for which payment is made.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers are prohibited from using CARCs and RARCs on remittance advice for payments made directly to participants, beneficiaries, or enrollees, including when the remittance advice is requested by the provider.

claims.quote: These final rules establish the general requirement that plans and issuers use CARCs and RARCs, in the manner and timeframe specified in guidance, to communicate information about whether an item or service identified on a claim is or is not subject to the surprise billing requirements under the No Surprises Act.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers are required to use CARCs and RARCs, in the manner and timeframe specified in guidance, to communicate information about whether an item or service identified on a claim is or is not subject to the surprise billing requirements under the No Surprises Act.

claims.quote: Future guidance will identify the specific CARCs and RARCs to be used in particular circumstances, which, as discussed below in section II.B.2.e of this preamble, when surprise billing protections do apply, may include use of CARCs and RARCs to communicate relevant procedural or administrative information related to application of the surprise billing protections to the items or services at issue.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers are required to use CARCs and RARCs to communicate relevant procedural or administrative information related to the application of surprise billing protections to items or services when such protections apply.

claims.quote: Future guidance will also provide any administrative and technical instructions necessary to facilitate the use of mandated CARCs and RARCs in all paper or electronic remittance advice transactions to providers that do not have a contractual relationship with the plan or issuer.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers are required to use mandated CARCs and RARCs in all paper or electronic remittance advice transactions to providers that do not have a contractual relationship with the plan or issuer.

claims.quote: Commenters recommended that any guidance should include explicit timelines for compliance and provide clear direction for how specified CARCs and RARCs must be used.
claims.summary: Guidance must include explicit timelines for compliance and provide clear direction for how specified CARCs and RARCs must be used.

claims.quote: Commenters requested that guidance address potential non-compliance, including describing oversight mechanisms and penalties and providing contact information for filing complaints against parties that are non-compliant with the CARC and RARC requirement.
claims.summary: Guidance must address potential non-compliance by describing oversight mechanisms and penalties and providing contact information for filing complaints against non-compliant parties.

claims.quote: The Departments have determined that guidance, rather than notice-and-comment rulemaking, is appropriate for providing the technical and operational instruction needed to implement this provision.
claims.summary: The Departments must use guidance rather than notice-and-comment rulemaking to provide technical and operational instruction for implementing the provision.

claims.quote: This approach will provide necessary flexibility, enabling the Departments to better respond to evolving needs and circumstances, including the flexibility to discontinue specification of certain CARCs and RARCs should the information they communicate become readily available to providers through a different mechanism or otherwise become unnecessary.
claims.summary: The Departments must maintain flexibility to discontinue specification of certain CARCs and RARCs if the information they communicate becomes readily available through a different mechanism or becomes unnecessary.

claims.quote: The Departments have determined that because all plans and issuers that provide ERA transactions that are subject to the HIPAA Administrative Simplification requirements are required to use CARCs and RARCs, most plans and issuers already have the capacity to implement the CARC and RARC requirement.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers that provide ERA transactions subject to HIPAA Administrative Simplification requirements are required to use CARCs and RARCs.

claims.quote: Plans and issuers will not be required to use CARCs and RARCs under these final rules until such date as provided for in future guidance.
claims.summary: Plans and issuers are not required to use CARCs and RARCs under these final rules until a future guidance date is provided.

claims.quote: the Departments will consider providing technical direction in future guidance to facilitate implementation of the CARC and RARC requirements on ERA with limited space available for data elements.
claims.summary: The Departments will consider providing technical direction in future guidance to facilitate implementation of the CARC and RARC requirements on ERA with limited space available for data elements.

The company shall file the following data with Treasury and shall transmit therewith the fee in accordance with the provisions of
claims.summary: Any company organized under the laws of the United States or of any state thereof, wishing to apply for recognition as an admitted reinsurer of surety companies doing business with the United States, must submit an application to Treasury, c/o Surety Bonds Program, to the location and in the manner specified online, and must file the following data with Treasury and transmit therewith the fee in accordance with the provisions of

claims.quote: This request must indicate: (A) The reason for applying for recognition; (B) Whether the company has ever previously applied for recognition as an admitted reinsurer, whether Treasury approved the application, and the applicable dates; and (C) If Treasury previously approved the company for recognition as an admitted reinsurer, the reason for termination of its recognition and the applicable date;
claims.summary: The request must indicate the reason for applying for recognition, whether the company has previously applied for recognition, whether Treasury approved the application, and the applicable dates, as well as the reason for termination of previous recognition and the applicable date.

claims.quote: A certified copy of its charter or articles of incorporation with all amendments as of the date of application showing the legal name of the company and that it is authorized to write reinsurance;
claims.summary: The company must provide a certified copy of its charter or articles of incorporation with all amendments as of the date of application, showing the legal name of the company and that it is authorized to write reinsurance.

claims.quote: A listing of the names of the company's current officers and directors as of the date of application, including a biographical affidavit of each officer and director per instructions online at https://www.fiscal.treasury.gov/surety-bonds/;
claims.summary: The company must provide a listing of the names of its current officers and directors as of the date of application, including a biographical affidavit of each officer and director per instructions online.

claims.quote: A certified copy of a license from any one state in which it has been authorized to do business showing its authority to write reinsurance and/or other lines of insurance;
claims.summary: The company must provide a certified copy of a license from any one state in which it has been authorized to do business, showing its authority to write reinsurance and/or other lines of insurance.

claims.quote: A copy of the latest available report of its examination by its domiciliary State Insurance Department including a copy of company responses to any significant findings or recommendations;
claims.summary: The company must provide a copy of the latest available report of its examination by its domiciliary State Insurance Department, including a copy of company responses to any significant findings or recommendations.

claims.quote: Annual statements of its financial condition, as of the close of the last two full years preceding the date of application, on the annual statement form of the NAIC with all Schedules and Exhibits completed, including copies of the NAIC File Upload, showing that it has paid-up capital of at least $250,000 in cash or its equivalent, in the case of a stock insurance company, or has net assets of not less than $500,000 over and above all liabilities, in the case of a mutual insurance company. The Annual Financial Statement's Jurat Page (only) is to be signed (facsimile signatures are acceptable) by the company President, Secretary, and a Notary Public who shall also affix a notary seal;
claims.summary: The company must provide annual statements of its financial condition, as of the close of the last two full years preceding the date of application, on the annual statement form of the NAIC with all Schedules and Exhibits completed, including copies of the NAIC File Upload, showing that it has paid-up capital of at least $250,000 in cash or its equivalent, or has net assets of not less than $500,000 over and above all liabilities. The Annual Financial Statement's Jurat Page (only) is to be signed by the company President, Secretary, and a Notary Public who shall also affix a notary seal.

claims.quote: IRIS ratio results, and an explanation for any ratios outside the normal ranges as established by the NAIC for the last two years preceding the date of application;
claims.summary: The company must provide IRIS ratio results and an explanation for any ratios outside the normal ranges as established by the NAIC for the last two years preceding the date of application.

claims.quote: A memorandum setting forth the company's method of operation, including lines of business written, the company's underwriting and claims philosophy, and significant changes in the company's operations or corporate structure that impact its financial statements;
claims.summary: The company must provide a memorandum setting forth its method of operation, including lines of business written, the company's underwriting and claims philosophy, and significant changes in its operations or corporate structure that impact its financial statements.

claims.quote: A completed Treasury Schedule F (Form No. TFS 6314), as referenced in § 223.9(c) for two years preceding the date of application;
claims.summary: The company must provide a completed Treasury Schedule F (Form No. TFS 6314), as referenced in § 223.9(c), for two years preceding the date of application.

claims.quote: A Statement of Actuarial Opinion as of the close of the last two years preceding the date of application provided by a qualified actuary, as defined by the NAIC, on the adequacy of all loss reserves with the scope and format of the statement also conforming to the requirements of the NAIC;
claims.summary: The company must provide a Statement of Actuarial Opinion as of the close of the last two years preceding the date of application, provided by a qualified actuary, as defined by the NAIC, on the adequacy of all loss reserves, with the scope and format of the statement also conforming to the requirements of the NAIC.

claims.quote: Such other evidence as Treasury may request to establish that the company is solvent and able to meet the continuing obligation to carry out its contracts.
claims.summary: The company must provide such other evidence as Treasury may request to establish that the company is solvent and able to meet the continuing obligation to carry out its contracts.

claims.quote: The submissions listed in paragraphs (h)(1)(i) through (xii) of this section, except that the financial statement of such branch shall show that it has net assets of not less than $250,000 over and above all liabilities;
claims.summary: The branch must submit financial statements showing net assets of not less than $250,000 over and above all liabilities.

claims.quote: Evidence satisfactory to Treasury to establish that it has on deposit in the United States not less than $250,000 available to its policyholders and creditors in the United States.
claims.summary: The branch must provide evidence satisfactory to Treasury to establish that it has on deposit in the United States not less than $25,000 available to its policyholders and creditors in the United States.

claims.quote: Any company recognized pursuant to paragraph (h)(1) or (2) of this section wishing to apply for renewal of its recognition shall submit an application to Treasury, c/o Surety Bonds Program, to the location, and in the manner, specified online at https://www.fiscal.treasury.gov/surety-bonds/.
claims.summary: A company recognized under paragraph (h)(1) or (2) must submit an application to Treasury, c/o Surety Bonds Program, to the location and in the manner specified online.

claims.quote: The company must file the following data with Treasury and shall transmit therewith the fee in accordance with the provisions of
claims.summary: The company must file the required data with Treasury and transmit the fee in accordance with the provisions.

claims.quote: Payment of the application fee in accordance with the provisions of
claims.summary: The company must pay the application fee in accordance with the provisions.

claims.quote: Annual statements of its financial condition, as of the close of the preceding year, on the annual statement form of the NAIC with all Schedules and Exhibits completed, including copies of the NAIC File Upload, showing that it has paid-up capital of at least $250,000 in cash or its equivalent, in the case of a stock insurance company, or has net assets of not less than $500,000 over and above all liabilities, in the case of a mutual insurance company.
claims.summary: The company must submit annual statements of its financial condition, as of the close of the preceding year, on the NAIC annual statement form with all Schedules and Exhibits completed, showing paid-up capital of at least $250,000 in cash or its equivalent, or net assets of not less than $500,000 over and above all liabilities.

claims.quote: The Annual Financial Statement's Jurat Page (only) is to be signed (facsimile signatures are acceptable) by the company President, Secretary, and a Notary Public who shall also affix a notary seal;
claims.summary: The Annual Financial Statement's Jurat Page must be signed by the company President, Secretary, and a Notary Public, with a notary seal affixed.

claims.quote: IRIS ratio results, and an explanation for any ratios outside the normal ranges as established by the NAIC as of the close of the preceding year;
claims.summary: The company must submit IRIS ratio results and an explanation for any ratios outside the normal ranges as established by the NAIC.

claims.quote: A completed Treasury Schedule F (Form No. TFS 6314), as referenced in
claims.summary: The company must submit a completed Treasury Schedule F (Form No. TFS 6314).

claims.quote: A listing of the names of the company's current officers and directors as of the close of the preceding year, including a biographical affidavit of each new officer and director per instructions online at https://www.fiscal.treasury.gov/surety-bonds/;
claims.summary: The company must submit a listing of the names of its current officers and directors as of the close of the preceding year, including a biographical affidavit for each new officer and director.

claims.quote: Such other evidence as Treasury may request to establish that the company is solvent and able to meet the continuing obligation to carry out its contracts.
claims.summary: The company must provide such other evidence as Treasury may request to establish that it is solvent and able to meet its continuing obligations.

claims.quote: Any company may apply for recognition as a complementary reinsurer or annual renewal of such recognition provided the company is licensed to write reinsurance by and has its head office in (or is domiciled in) a non-U.S. jurisdiction that is subject to an in-force Covered Agreement entered into with the United States pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 313-314, which Covered Agreement addresses the elimination, under specified conditions, of collateral requirements as a condition for entering into any reinsurance agreement with a ceding insurer domiciled in a U.S. state or for allowing the ceding insurer to recognize credit for reinsurance.
claims.summary: A company may apply for recognition as a complementary reinsurer or annual renewal of such recognition if it is licensed to write reinsurance, has its head office in a non-U.S. jurisdiction subject to an in-force Covered Agreement, and the agreement addresses the elimination of collateral requirements.

claims.quote: To obtain recognition as a complementary reinsurer, the company must submit to Treasury the fee in accordance with the provisions of
claims.summary: To obtain recognition as a complementary reinsurer, the company must submit the fee in accordance with the provisions.

claims.quote: Meet and maintain all capital and surplus, solvency, and market conduct requirements under the applicable Covered Agreement;
claims.summary: The party must meet and maintain all capital and surplus, solvency, and market conduct requirements under the applicable Covered Agreement.

claims.quote: Be recognized by at least one U.S. state as a Reciprocal Jurisdiction Reinsurer, as defined by the state's credit for reinsurance law or regulation based on the NAIC's Credit for Reinsurance Model Law and Regulation, and submit proof of such recognition;
claims.summary: The party must be recognized by at least one U.S. state as a Reciprocal Jurisdiction Reinsurer and submit proof of such recognition.

claims.quote: Submit to Treasury: (i) For initial applications for recognition, all information provided by the company or by the supervisory authority of the company's domiciliary jurisdiction to any U.S. state regulator in the two most recently completed calendar years. (ii) For applications for renewal of recognition, all semi-annual and annual filing information provided by the company or by the supervisory authority of the company's domiciliary jurisdiction to any U.S. state regulator in the most recently completed calendar year. (iii) Payment of the application fee in accordance with the provisions of
claims.summary: The party must submit to Treasury: (i) For initial applications for recognition, all information provided by the company or by the supervisory authority of the company's domiciliary jurisdiction to any U.S. state regulator in the two most recently completed calendar years; (ii) For applications for renewal of recognition, all semi-annual and annual filing information provided by the company or by the supervisory authority of the company's domiciliary jurisdiction to any U.S. state regulator in the most recently completed calendar year; (iii) Payment of the application fee in accordance with the provisions of § 223.22.

claims.quote: Any company may apply for recognition or annual renewal of such recognition as an alien reinsurer, provided it is licensed to write reinsurance by, and has its head office or domicile in, a non-U.S. jurisdiction that is recognized by a U.S. state as a Qualified Jurisdiction or as a Reciprocal Jurisdiction, provided that the Reciprocal Jurisdiction is not party to an in-force Covered Agreement as described in paragraph (i) of this section.
